reference.source: Haematology references / bone marrow failure guidelines
clinicalPearls: Pancytopenia with a hypocellular bone marrow in the absence of an abnormal infiltrate or fibrosis
Presents with anaemia, bleeding from thrombocytopenia and infection from neutropenia
Most acquired cases are immune-mediated; others follow drugs, toxins, viral infection or radiation
Inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (for example Fanconi anaemia, dyskeratosis congenita) must be excluded, especially in the young
Severity is graded by blood counts and marrow cellularity, guiding urgency of treatment
Treatment is immunosuppressive therapy or, for suitable patients, allogeneic stem cell transplantation, with supportive transfusion and infection control
reference.pathophysiology: Acquired aplastic anaemia is most often an immune-mediated disorder in which cytotoxic T lymphocytes attack haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, causing their depletion and a markedly hypocellular marrow with resulting pancytopenia. Triggers include certain drugs, toxins (such as benzene), viral infections and, rarely, radiation, though many cases are idiopathic. A minority arise from inherited defects of stem cell maintenance or DNA repair (inherited bone marrow failure syndromes), and there is overlap with clonal disorders such as paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and myelodysplasia.
additionalDifferentials: Inherited bone marrow failure (Fanconi anaemia, dyskeratosis congenita)
Megaloblastic anaemia or drug-induced marrow suppression
additionalInvestigations: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine showing hypocellularity
Cytogenetics and flow cytometry (including PNH clone testing)
Chromosome breakage or telomere studies where inherited syndromes are suspected
Screening for viral and drug causes
redFlags: Features suggesting an inherited syndrome or evolving clonal disorder
reference.prognosis: Severe untreated aplastic anaemia is life-threatening, but immunosuppressive therapy and, especially, matched allogeneic transplantation achieve good long-term survival in many patients; clonal evolution remains a long-term risk.
pitfalls: Missing an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome, which changes management
Overlooking a PNH clone or evolving myelodysplasia
Attributing pancytopenia to aplasia without excluding marrow infiltration
Delaying definitive therapy in severe disease
